item.title: France protests escalating into riots are a political gift for Marine Le Pen and far-right
item.description: Ahead of the April 2027 presidential elections, far-right politicians have vowed to deport ‘illegal’ migrants, increase police funding and discipline students.
item.content:encoded:
Mass protests in France have spiralled into riots, with between 500,000 and 800,000 demonstrators in cities and towns across the country, most of them students. More than 100 police and many more protesters have been injured and up to 2,000 people have so far been arrested.

Major public buildings – such as the town hall in Limoges and the historic tourist office in Lyon – were destroyed, while other public buildings were damaged and hundreds of shops were looted by small groups of mainly young men.

The protests began in the working-class suburb of Créteil in southeastern Paris on September 21 when high school students demonstrated against poor conditions: dilapidated facilities, a shortage of teachers and inconvenient timetabling (schools in France often spread classes between 8am and 6pm, including Saturday mornings, leaving one clear afternoon).

This summer’s heatwaves were still being felt in September in classrooms with no cooling systems. Senior school students have been further frustrated by the inefficiencies and inequities of the Parcoursup university application online portal.

item.title: Odisha: Two activists held in case linked to April clash between police, residents over Vedanta mine
item.description: Randall Sequeira and Laxman Naik have not been named in the first information report filed in connection with the incident, activists alleged.
item.content:encoded:
Two activists working with Adivasi and Dalit communities in southern Odisha were arrested in Bhawanipatna town in Kalahandi district on Friday in connection with a case linked to an April clash between police and residents in the Rayagada district.

Randall Sequeira and Laxman Naik were taken from Sequeira’s home in Hill Town at around 10.45 pm, activists and the Right to Food Campaign said.

The police allegedly seized their mobile phones and took them to the Town Police Station without explaining the grounds for their arrest or producing a warrant.

The two were reportedly kept in custody overnight without access to their lawyers or families. They were taken to Rayagada the following day and produced before a sub-divisional judicial magistrate at around 6.30 pm, after which they were sent to the Rayagada Sub Jail, Countercurrents reported.

Neither Sequeira nor Naik is named in the first information report related to the April incident, the activists have alleged.

April clashes

The case relates to a clash in Kantamal on the night of April 6 and April 7, when police entered a village in Rayagada, amid protests against a road project linked to Vedanta Limited’s proposed Sijimali bauxite mine.

item.title: ‘Why am I so aloof and lost these days?’: These poems grieve and celebrate a distant beloved
item.description: An excerpt from ‘O’ Beloved, The Heart Sings’, by Madhu Kailas.
item.content:encoded:
Every night I starve and pine,
Looking at the moon and its light.
I hear from the wayfarers who have seen her,
That my beloved is more beautiful than the moon.


Because I have nothing to offer her,
Because I do not know how to reach her heart,
My heart loves her with the last drop of blood
Just to keep itself alive.


Amid an ominous, murderous thunderstorm
I could only see my beloved’s face
Reflected in piercing flashes of lightning strikes,
Ripping apart my anguished heart.


After the rains we stepped out of the shelter,
The scent of wet earth consumed us.
I touched my beloved’s hand gently like a feather,
The beads of water had turned to pearls on her form.


One more sunset, the birds are returning home.
I clean the soot off the glass lamps with much care.
My beloved’s face glows everywhere in the dark,
I light the lamps, one by one, to dispel her thoughts.


I dare not ask myself: why am I so aloof and lost these days?
This world has become an empty shell.
Why is it then, that my beloved’s name
rests on the tip of my heart like a prayer?


The letters never arrived.

item.title: India at growing risk of infectious diseases due to climate change effects
item.description: Excess rainfall allows bacteria and viruses to thrive and spread while drought-like conditions can intensify transmission and hygiene dangers.
item.content:encoded:
When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat.

Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of disease-carrying insects and bring people, animals and pathogens into closer contact, increasing the risk of outbreaks in new places at unexpected times.

The latest assessment report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that heatwaves and extreme rainfall events are projected to increase in the coming years.

A 2025 study by IPE Global, an international development consultancy, and Esri India, a GIS mapping company, warns that extreme weather could become more severe by 2030, with heatwaves projected to double in major cities and extreme rainfall events expected to rise by 43% across the country.

Health experts state that we need to factor in and prevent climate-related outbreaks rather than simply responding to them.

Monsoon and drought risk

The World Meteorological Organisation reports that the past decade has witnessed some of the worst floods on record. India, too, has experienced devastating floods, including those in Mumbai in 2025 and Kerala in 2018.

item.title: CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das’ judicial custody extended by two days
item.description: Ranka and Das, along with another campaign leader were detained on October 13 after they ‘sneaked into’ Jantar Mantar and waved the national flag.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Monday extended by two days the judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, Bar and Bench reported.

The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Wednesday.

Ranka and Das, along with another campaign leader, Ajinkya Shinde, were detained on October 13 after they trespassed on Jantar Mantar and waved the national flag. They had “sneaked into” the Jantar Mantar to oppose the authorities’ decision to denotify the area as a designated protest site.

On October 14, Ranka and Das were sent to judicial custody for five days. Shinde was released on a personal bond.

After the custody period ended on Monday, they were produced before a special executive magistrate, where the Delhi Police sought an extension, Bar and Bench reported.

The magistrate allowed the request, extending their judicial custody by two more days.

Cockroach Janta Party leader Ratna Singh described the decision as a “mockery of the justice system”.

Abhik Chimni, the lawyer representing the CJP leaders, said that the proceedings were preventive in nature and that the court had itself observed that there was no need to send them to judicial custody.

item.title: Manipur: Protesters place bodies of two men killed in fresh violence outside CM’s home
item.description: Three persons were killed and three injured after a group of firewood collectors came under fire near the boundary of Imphal East and Kangpokpi districts.
item.content:encoded:
Protesters in Manipur on Monday placed the bodies of two men outside Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh’s home in Imphal after they were killed by suspected militants near the border of Imphal East and Kangpokpi districts.

Imphal East is predominantly inhabited by Meiteis, while Kangpokpi is a Kuki-majority district.

A group had brought the bodies to Imphal to protest the continuing violence in the state since 2023. An eyewitness told Scroll that the police fired several rounds of tear gas to disperse the protesters, following which the bodies were taken to the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences.

The two persons who died were identified as 35-year-old Arubam Ronil and 51-year-old Lairenlakpam Inaobi. They were among a group of firewood collectors who came under fire near the boundary of Imphal East and Kangpokpi districts. Four persons were injured in the attack.

One of the injured men, 32-year-old Ksh Sushil later succumbed to his injuries taking the toll to three in the incident.

Ethnic clashes had first broken out in Manipur in May 2023 between the Meitei and the Kuki-Zo-Hmar communities.

The advisory, seen by Scroll, was issued amid protests in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over concerns about the Election Commission and its handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

In the advisory dated October 10, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology asked Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, to “provide adequate context in relation to photographs, videos, graphics or other content depicting ongoing public events”.

It said that content allowed to be shared without such context “may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquility”.

Bora, the president of the All India Students’ Association, was detained on Friday while participating in a flash protest by the student group near Barakhamba Road demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The student leader has alleged that they were taken to an undisclosed location and later to the RK Puram Police Station. Bora was held at the police station overnight before being released at 6 am, the following day.

item.title: Fiction: Friendship blossoms when five women find one another at different crossroads in their lives
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Un-Wife Club’, by Akriti Tyagi.
item.content:encoded:
Mira Rao had a sinking suspicion that wedding receptions were God’s way of saying, “Let’s remind you, you’re still single!” And this one was a masterpiece in emotional torture. She wasn’t sure what was worse – that she’d seen her ex-husband at the wedding she could barely afford to attend, or that he hadn’t even noticed her.

“Unbelievable,” she muttered under her breath, clutching her wine glass like it might give her the superpowers she desperately needed. Her eyes flickered over the twinkling fairy lights strung above the setting as she took in the laughter of love-struck couples swirling around her like confetti. It was like every romcom she had ever despised had come to life, with her playing the role of the awkward, unnoticed extra.

She adjusted her sari, the deep teal fabric pulling a little too tightly around her waist, as though mocking her attempt at composure. item.title: Fear of false declaration for using new voter registration form after SIR exclusion is misplaced: HC
item.description: The court noted that the EC suggested using Form 6, meant for first-time voter registration, to restore names deleted during the SIR.
item.content:encoded:
The Delhi High Court has said that a voter’s apprehension of being accused of making a false declaration by submitting Form 6 to restore his name to the electoral roll after being excluded during the special intensive revision was “misplaced” since the direction to do so had come from the Election Commission, Bar and Bench reported on Monday. Form 6 is meant for first-time voter registration.

The court made the observation while closing a petition filed by two persons whose names were deleted from the draft electoral roll in Delhi after they could not complete the SIR enumeration process following a change of residence.

The petitioners had challenged the poll panel’s direction requiring existing electors who were left out during the SIR to seek fresh inclusion through Form 6, rather than use Form 8 to correct or shift their existing electoral entries.

Form 8 is meant for shifting residence and correcting details in an existing electoral roll.

They sought to have their names restored to the electoral roll and moved to the constituency where they now lived.

The poll panel told the court that the petitioners could seek the restoration of their names by submitting Form 6.

However, the petitioners submitted that furnishing Form 6 would amount to making a false declaration.

item.title: How Sufi shrines became architectural manifestations of Islam’s notions of beauty and art
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Knots in Time: Sufism and Shrines’ by Ali Khan Mahmudabad in ‘Spiritual India: A Kaleidoscope of Faith’, edited by Briana Blasko.
item.content:encoded:
“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The Parable of His Light is as if there were a Niche and within it a Lamp: the Lamp enclosed in Glass: the glass as it were a brilliant star: Lit from a blessed Tree, an Olive, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil is well-nigh luminous, though fire scarce touched it: Light upon Light! Allah doth guide whom He will to His Light: Allah doth set forth Parables for men: and Allah doth know all things.”

He who knows himself, surely, knows God.

Although there is much academic debate about the origins of Sufism – the mystical branch of Islam – it is widely accepted by Muslims that, in its essence, Sufism is firmly grounded in the Quran and the Hadith. Today, Sufism is largely only associated with the esoteric and mystical aspects of Islam. However, in the pre-modern Muslim world, Sufism was not just about these aspects of the religion, but was an inextricable part of everyday practice – as both religion and mysticism were integrated into all aspects of life, be it art and craft, architecture, poetry, music, social and material culture, and even political resistance. item.title: Cheaper cancer medication: Kerala HC ruling is an opportunity for Centre to take the lead
item.description: While considering access to two patented breast cancer drugs, the court has recognised that high costs can warrant government intervention.
item.content:encoded:
When I was diagnosed with breast cancer last year, I faced the challenge of weighing both the cost of treatment and the treatment itself. I did not have substantial insurance or savings, but family and friends came forward to help.

During treatment, I met other women who lacked the same support. For some, paying for care was a continuing struggle, especially when it stretched over several months. I wondered whether some of those who stopped coming were forced to choose between the treatment they needed and what they could afford.

The question of what happens when a cancer medicine is simply too expensive came up before the Kerala High Court on September 26. In the case of Re Exorbitant Pricing of Life Saving Patented Medicines vs Union of India, the court considered access to two patented breast cancer medicines – ribociclib and abemaciclib.

A retired bank employee living with metastatic breast cancer had approached the court in 2022 seeking affordable access to ribociclib. Though she died while the case was pending, the court continued the case on its own motion.

item.title: A new book explores the ethical and existential challenges of AI and how humans respond to them
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Will AI Murder Us All?: The Moral Psychology of Artificial Intelligence’, by Aakash Singh Rathore.
item.content:encoded:
The apocalypse unfolding around artificial intelligence is not only planetary and systemic, but also intimate, reshaping what it means to be a person in the world.

The first horse rides in through our screens. Physical presence: seeing, touching, smelling the other has been steadily displaced by mediated interaction in the virtual, the digital and the metaverse. The smartphone always gestured towards this destination; Covid merely revealed it. What once felt like an intrusion now feels natural. We used to protest cameras in public spaces; today, we pose and sit before them voluntarily, for hours each day, curating our own surveillance. AI hoovers in every image, for data, for training, for selling, for supremacy and control.

The second horse follows close behind: total surveillance. Governments and corporations no longer simply know where we are, but where we are going, what we own and what we are likely to desire next. What we say (or type) is aggregated into what we think (via AI-generated predictive text). Keep in mind, when we transit from disembodied AI to physical droids, passive surveillance seamlessly slips into active control … policing, internment, god only knows!

item.title: Why Modi government’s rural jobs scheme is a sham in drought-hit Maharashtra district
item.description: On paper, thousands are getting work under the scheme in Beed. But Scroll’s investigation found ghost workers, half-built roads and lakhs paid in wages.
item.content:encoded:
October in Maharashtra’s Beed district is usually a time of hope. Reservoirs and wells are filled to the brim, fields of soybean and cotton are about to be harvested.

But this year, there is neither water nor work in this Marathwada region.

The crisis is widespread. More than two-thirds of Maharashtra – 304 out of 358 tehsils – have been declared drought-hit after recording an 18% deficit in monsoon rains. In Beed, the deficit went up to 37%, making it the worst in a decade, said collector Vivek Johnson.

The lack of rainfall in July, August and September shrunk the soybean crop on Satish Shirsath’s one-acre plot of land in Chumbali village. The seeds he harvested were so tiny that they fetched only Rs 10,000 in the market, not enough to recover the investment of Rs 20,000.

When the crop failed, Shirsath began to look for work.

In August, India’s newly revamped rural employment guarantee scheme came to his aid. He earned Rs 3,000 after digging a canal for six days under the Viksit Bharat- Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) or VB-G RAM G scheme.

But since then, Shirsath has not found any work.

item.title: How singer Nina Simone worked with poet Langston Hughes to put a spell on listeners
item.description: Beyond using his considerable fame to elevate Simone, Hughes also inspired her songwriting.
item.content:encoded:
Many music fans know that Nina Simone’s 1965 hit I Put a Spell on You helped establish the 32-year-old singer as the “High Priestess of Soul.”

Few probably realise that it was Langston Hughes – the pioneering poet and face of the Harlem Renaissance – who had encouraged Simone to record it.

As a Langston Hughes scholar, I’ve spent the past six years documenting Hughes’ largely overlooked friendship with Simone. I explore the creative bond they shared in my newest book, “Don’t Let Me Be Misunderstood: Nina Simone, Langston Hughes, and the Birth of Black Power, which details how the two supported and inspired each other.

The seeds of this relationship were planted in 1949, when Hughes delivered a lecture featuring his own poetry at Simone’s high school in Asheville, North Carolina. Simone – then known by her birth name, Eunice Waymon – was just 16 years old.

As part of the programming, Simone played the piano. Hughes was impressed. Even though she was just a teenager, Hughes saw her as a “somebody” – a budding talent who would one day join figures such as classical singer Marian Anderson in the pantheon of legendary Black performance artists. item.title: CEC protests: Several detained during ‘Tiranga March’ in Mumbai
item.description: Some protesters were not allowed to leave the place they were staying at ahead of the demonstration, a Cockroach Janta Party volunteer alleged.
item.content:encoded:
The Mumbai Police on Friday detained several persons who had gathered for a “Tiranga March” at Carter Road in Bandra, the Cockroach Janta Party has alleged.

item.title: ‘The Future Is Peace’: A Palestinian‑Israeli memoir seeks to break the cycle of violence
item.description: The memoir stands out as a rare work of true, focused resolution, which highlights the shared humanity at the heart of an intractable conflict.
item.content:encoded:
Since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, the world has witnessed unimaginable, almost constant violence in Gaza and the West Bank. But people’s understanding of these events is not universal – each person is exposed to a particular set of narratives surrounding history, victimhood and trauma.

The vast majority of news reports, social media posts, videos, and books that have covered the events since October 7, 2023 can be defined as what I call “conflict media”, which reproduces the divisions of the conflict it describes, perpetuating it to the point where the media itself becomes a weapon in an information war.

As a scholar of the Middle East, I have rarely – though not never – encountered conflict media’s opposite, which I call “resolution media”.

The most famous works of resolution media have emerged after a conflict ends, and highlight the universal suffering of war. item.title: India and Pakistan have forgotten the most enduring lesson of the Cuban missile crisis
item.description: After the dangerous escalation in May 2025, the world cannot afford another confrontation in Southasia which tests assumptions that fortuitously survived once.
item.content:encoded:
At the height of the Cuban missile crisis, American warships dropped small explosive charges near a Soviet submarine off the coast of Cuba on October 27, 1962. Their purpose was to force the B-59 submarine to surface. The Americans did not know that it carried a nuclear torpedo. Inside the submarine, officers who had been cut off from reliable communications struggled to determine whether war had begun.

Captain Valentin Savitsky came close to ordering the torpedo’s use but another senior officer aboard, Vasili Arkhipov, helped prevent that decision. The episode was fully understood decades later, a reminder of how close the world came to the use of nuclear weapons through misperception, incomplete information, and compressed decision timelines under stress.

The incident, dramatised in The Man Who Saved the World, a 2012 television documentary in the PBS series Secrets of the Dead series, illustrates how nuclear escalation can begin without either belligerent choosing to go nuclear. One side conducts an operation it considers limited while the other encounters explosions, incomplete information and uncertainty about what will happen next. Decisions then depend on officers under tremendous pressure, interpreting intentions they cannot verify.

He repeated to himself “She’s only a woman” with the objective indifference of a connoisseur. But one moment later, unable to bear his mother’s unawareness or his own attentions, he wanted to shout, “Cover yourself, stop showing yourself to me, I’m not who I used to be.”

Thirteen-year-old Agostino and his widowed mother are visiting the beach for the summer. Lithuanian writer Jaroslavas Melnikas writes from the edge of certainty. His fictional world is one where reality constantly slips into another, where ordinary lives suddenly confront metaphysical doubt, and where human beings stand suspended between the visible and the invisible. I was drawn to this unsettling world long before I began translating The Last Day into Hindi. These stories not only captivated my literary sensibility but also led me toward self-reflection.

The paradoxes and predicaments faced by the characters in this collection were deeply rooted in human consciousness. Melnikas’ characters inhabit unstable realities where everyday life suddenly fractures, exposing loneliness, moral ambiguity, and the fragility of certainty. When Ravi Shemesh’s uncle died recently, the family cooked pappu charu.

It is a sour lentil broth, made frequently in nearly every household in coastal Andhra Pradesh.

The Shemesh family made it in a large pot on the fire in the yard, on a mud and brick stove, wood underneath. It was served to all the relatives after the funeral.

There was another kitchen in the house, indoors, with fitted cupboards and a granite worktop and a gas hob, and that was where Ravi’s mother rolls and griddles the chapatis. But the big pots go outside, on the fire.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: India’s classical music unites faiths. Its syncretic heritage must be preserved
item.description: More than any other field, it is classical music where Hindus and Muslims have lived, worked, laboured and created together.
item.content:encoded:
Some 20 years ago, I was in Lahore for an academic conference, where I met an aspiring classical vocalist who travelled every week to learn from a teacher in Karachi. Though I cannot hold a note myself, I have had a lifelong love for Hindustani music. I was thus surprised to learn from this talented Pakistani singer that his teacher spoke derisively of a particular raga as one that “belonged to the Hindus” (woh toh Hinduon ka raga hai).

I didn’t have the heart to tell the young man that such distinctions did not exist among classical musicians in India, or that a singer he admired, Roshanara Begum, had continued to sing the ragas, Shankara and Durga, after she moved to Pakistan even though they were named for Hindu deities. I could also have mentioned Salamat Ali Khan’s rendition of Nadiya Kinare Mora Gaon where this singer (who also lived in Pakistan) explains that the thumri is based on the love of Radha for Krishna.

Admittedly, both Roshanara and Salamat were born well before Partition when such seamless interchange of ideas and motifs between different faiths was part of the musical culture of undivided India.

item.title: Data shows 73% decline in world’s wildlife population – and more animals are not being counted

Wildlife populations around the world have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. That’s according to the WWF’s new 2026 Living Planet Index – a major estimate, updated every two years, of the changing state of nature. This does not mean that 73% of the world’s animals have disappeared. Rather, it is the average decline in the size of wildlife populations that is being monitored.

The index is one of the metrics used to track progress towards the UN’s biodiversity goals and shapes narratives of biodiversity loss across the world. But the data behind that 73% headline, one of the most comprehensive available, is still far from complete.

Very few, outside of those of us working at the coalface of handling biodiversity data, understand just how poorly wild animal populations are monitored. Though the world faces the joint crises of climate change and biodiversity loss, we can track climate change through thousands of weather stations or measures of atmospheric CO₂. Biodiversity is far harder to measure. Counting wildlife is highly resource intensive, generally can’t be done from space, and systematic monitoring is extremely patchy.

item.content:encoded:
“Twenty years ago, all this was paddy,” says Nazir Ahmad, a farmer from Qaimoh, a village in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district, pointing at the rows of apple saplings that now cover his land. Today, much of that landscape has changed. The irrigation channels set up for paddy still exist, running through the fields as they always have. However, the paddy they once fed has given way to apple plantations.

item.title: ‘I wrote a children’s book about an insult I faced. Later, I had the same thought about my daughter’
item.description: Tamil American novelist and essayist Lakshmi Iyer on ‘colourism’.

I typed the word and stopped. Kaali. Two syllables, said by a grandmother to a 12-year-old, in a book meant for readers who are ten. The cursor blinked after the i. Outside, the school bus trundled past our home. I was relieved to get away from my manuscript to make coffee for the kids. Excavating memories is never fun.

Kaali. Black one. Dark one. Is it a slur? Kaali is an adjective, a nickname. It masquerades as concern. It comes from the people who love you, over breakfast, with a palm against your cheek.

‘Even though she is dark, she glows’

I know this because I was that child. Sixth grade, maybe seventh, and Amma is mixing kadalai maavu with paal yedu and a pinch of manjal podi, spreading the creamy paste across my face, waiting for it to dry to a crust before washing it off. I quite enjoyed the ritual, the feeling of amma’s soft palms against my cheek, the chill of the paste evaporating from the heat of my skin, the film tightening the skin until it stretched and you could no longer smile or speak. item.title: How photography helped physicist Bibha Chowdhuri see the invisible in the 1930s
item.description: The scientist used light-sensitive plates to trace cosmic particles, contributing to pioneering research in particle physics.
item.content:encoded:
In 1939, a 26-year-old physicist published an article that contains what, at first, reads like instructions for an eccentric treasure hunt: place photographic plates in a refrigerator in Calcutta, in Darjeeling or in a Dak Bungalow at Sandakphu. But Bibha Chowdhuri was not looking for buried treasure. She was looking for traces of the invisible.

The plates had been prepared with samarium sulphate and exposed for months to cosmic radiation. When two of those placed at Sandakphu were developed, they revealed 30 “star-like tracks” – microscopic records of nuclear disintegration. The photographs transformed an otherwise invisible encounter between cosmic rays and matter into something that could be seen and studied.

Chowdhuri’s experiment belonged to a new kind of scientific image-making, pioneered in part by physicist Marietta Blau, in which photographic emulsions became detectors of subatomic events. Working with DM Bose at Calcutta’s Bose Institute, Chowdhuri would go on to develop methods for distinguishing particles by the tracks they left in photographic plates. Her work formed part of a chain of experiments that culminated in Cecil Powell’s Nobel Prize-winning research on mesotrons.

item.title: ‘How to Date a Fanatic’: Aruni Kashyap’s new novel is hopeful of getting a more tolerant India

item.content:encoded:
While reading Aruni Kashyap’s second novel, How to Date a Fanatic, I was confronted with a curious and delicious problem – how does one slot this novel and the novelist? When Kashyap debuted with A House with a Thousand Stories in 2013, a coming-of-age story about young Pablo set against the backdrop of insurgency, the novel could firmly be located in Mayong, Kashyap’s hometown in Assam, and in the tradition of Assamese novelists writing in English.

With the publication of his collection of short stories, His Father’s Disease, in 2019, one noted an expansion, both in terms of the geographical location that extended from Assam to Minnesota and its thematic preoccupation with violence, both personal and political, that stretched to explore issues of identity, sexuality, racism and belonging.

But with his latest novel, Kashyap seems to have shattered barriers of regionalism and set expectations for the writer belonging to the North East, the stranglehold of both of which he had scathingly critiqued in his short story “Skylark Girl,” to write a novel that compels you to place his writing on a wider, even planetary map.

Comics have been making their way into museums and art galleries for a while now. Over the last couple of years alone, Kolkata mounted an exhibition on the material craft of comics on the heels of a historical survey of Bengali comics from the 1920s to the present. Delhi’s Kiran Nadar Museum of Art turned itself into an embodied romp across the history of comics, inexplicably buffeted on both sides by a live archive of zines. All this alongside the Comic Cons trudging along each year while the Indie Comix Fests undyingly hop across cities as an open-source, comics-focused alternative.

Cartoonist Amruta Patil’s new exhibition A Moving Line, which opened at MAP Bengaluru on July 24, brings together more than 250 works spanning artefacts across millennia: temple carvings from Bengaluru’s own Someshwara temple to kaavad shrines and pattachitra scrolls; from the Tagore family’s early experiments with social caricature and the Ray family’s patronage for Sandesh to Amar Chitra Katha and Tinkle; from the deflatingly satirical strips of Bengal’s Basantak to glimpses of Pran’s Chacha Chaudhary and Falah Faisal’s Musalman; from thousands of webcomics blooming across platforms to the ongoing boom in graphic novels. Across France, school students have taken to the streets to protest about teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and long school days.

While the tradition of student protest has long roots in France, the country’s current fiscal crisis combined with entrenched structural problems with teacher recruitment, sickness absence and a backlog of school maintenance means this is unlikely to be something the current government can easily address.

Problems – and protests – regarding conditions in French schools go back decades.

The per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices is $2,886 against India’s $2,749, according to long-term data and forecasts in IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook published on October 13.

In 2027, Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product is estimated to be $3,219, ahead of India’s $3,036, the data showed. Bangladesh will maintain the marginal lead in 2028.

When many people think of an average lung cancer patient, they often imagine an older man smoking. But the face of lung cancer has changed. Over the past 15 years, more women, never smokers and younger people are being diagnosed with lung cancer.

In fact, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women, and more women die from lung cancer than breast, ovarian and colorectal cancer each year. The American Lung Association reports that while lung cancer rates have risen by 79% for women over the last 44 years, they decreased by 43% for men. item.title: India’s small steelmakers struggle to go green
item.description: The ‘secondary’ steel sector operates on tight margins but is crucial for the economy and supplies metal to key industries.
item.content:encoded:
The steel industry announces itself early on the road from Raipur airport into the city. Hoardings for Goel TMT, GK TMT, Concrete TMT and many others appear one after another. These steel brands are deeply interwoven with Chhattisgarh’s economy but are barely known outside the state.

Farther out, towards the industrial clusters of Urla and Siltara, the advertisements give way to the plants themselves: ironmaking units, rolling mills, steel-melting shops, trucks carrying coal and iron ore, and stacks of steel bars and tubes waiting to be transported across the country. The air changes, too, thick with smoke and dust. The environmental cost of steelmaking is difficult to miss, but so is its economic importance.

These industrial clusters support tens of thousands of workers and a much larger network of transporters, traders, contractors and small suppliers. They also reflect a wider reality across India.

The micro, small and medium-size enterprises that largely make up the “secondary” steel sector are responsible for around 40% of crude steel production in India, the world’s second-largest steelmaking nation. item.title: ‘Why then this fear of owls / Calling in the night?’: New nature poems by Ruskin Bond
item.description: An excerpt from ‘I Was the Wind Last Night: New and Selected Poems’, by Ruskin Bond.
item.content:encoded:
Cherry Tree

Eight years have passed
Since I placed my cherry seed in the grass.
“Must have a tree of my own,” I said—
And watered it once and went to bed
And forgot; but cherries have a way of growing
Though no one’s caring very much or knowing,
And suddenly that summer, near the end of May,
I found a tree had come to stay.
It was very small, a five months’ child,
Lost in the tall grass running wild.
Goats ate the leaves, a grasscutter’s scythe
Split it apart, and a monsoon blight
Shrivelled the slender stem… Even so,
Next spring I watched three new shoots grow,
The young tree struggle, upwards thrust
Its arms in a fresh fierce lust
For light and air and sun.
I could only wait, as one
Who watches, wondering, while
Time and the rain
Made a miracle from green, growing pain…

I went away next year—
Spent a season in Kashmir—
Came back thinner, rather poor,
But richer by a cherry tree at my door.
Six feet high, my own dark cherry,

Ripened and jewelled in the sun,
Hung from a branch – just one!

item.title: Persons converting to Islam cannot claim Backward Class Muslim status, says SC
item.description: On March 24, the Supreme Court said that only persons belonging to the Hindu, Buddhist and Sikh faiths can claim the Scheduled Caste status.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a Madras High Court ruling that said that a person from the Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes, Denotified Communities and Scheduled Castes who converts to Islam cannot claim reservations under the Backward Class (Muslim) category, Bar and Bench reported.

On June 24, the High Court struck down a Tamil Nadu government order, after which the state challenged it in July.

On Thursday, the bench said that a person who converts to Islam does not automatically become a member of one of the seven notified backward class social communities in the state, Live Law reported.

“His former caste status cannot be transposed to the Muslim backward class category, nor can his private religious body conclusively determine such status entitlement,” it said.

On March 24, the Supreme Court said that only persons belonging to the Hindu, Buddhist and Sikh faiths can claim the Scheduled Caste status. A Dalit person converting to any religion other than the three loses his or her Scheduled Caste status, regardless of the status at birth, the court had ruled at the time, citing Clause 3 of the 1950 Constitution Scheduled Caste Order.

The Indian Army and Air Force were already primed for action and thus wasted no time. The first aircraft, a Dakota DC-3, carrying a company of valiant Sikhs under Lieutenant Colonel Dewan Ranjit Rai roared into the sky from Gurgaon to rescue a beleaguered state on October 27, 1947, from Palam. There was a Madras Battalion stationed there too, but it was commanded by a British officer, so the honour of being the first troops to fly to defend Srinagar fell on one Sikh.

The police issued a Leave India Notice after Khan had taken part in the agitation at August Kranti Maidan in Mumbai on Saturday “despite not being an Indian citizen”, the news agency reported.

A Leave India Notice is a directive issued by the authorities requiring a foreign citizen to exit the country within a specified time period. Failing to comply with the order could lead to detention, deportation or blacklisting.

Khan is a citizen of the United States and holds an Overseas Citizen of India card, Hindustan Times reported.

Overseas Citizen of India is an immigration status that allows foreign citizens of Indian origin to live and work in India indefinitely.

The police have initiated action against him under the Immigration Act, the newspaper reported.
